children: East African airlines are pinning their hopes on Aliko Dangote’s planned oil refinery in Lamu, Kenya, in the hope of securing a new source of jet fuel and reducing their exposure to external supply shocks.

This came as the Middle East crisis pushed up the cost of aviation fuel and exposed the region’s dependence on supplies from outside Africa. The African Airlines Association (AFRAA), which negotiates jet fuel prices for all African airlines, says that Dangote’s entry into the jet A-1 fuel business has ensured some supply security on the continent and that his expansion into East Africa could benefit the region’s airlines.

This year, airlines in the region, both large and small, have grappled with soaring fuel costs and supply constraints due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war on Iran, which has significantly reduced their profit margins.

Abderahmane Berthe, Afraa’s secretary-general, told The EastAfrican that the refinery offers a ‘African solution’ to the fuel challenges facing regional airlines, providing not only supply security but also lower costs. “That will reduce costs and also avoid the crisis we are seeing because of fuel coming from other regions,” he said in an interview at the Aviation Africa Summit last week.

Over the past six months, airlines in the region have been hit particularly hard by the global surge in fuel costs, which has disproportionately impacted Africa. This has pushed up their operating costs and reduced their profit margins.
According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), the price of jet fuel in Africa has more than doubled to $190 per barrel since the start of the conflict in Iran in February.
African airlines now pay the second-highest fuel prices after European carriers, who currently pay $192.38 per barrel. Meanwhile, the Middle East enjoys the lowest prices, at $164 per barrel.

Read: Uganda’s domestic airlines raise fares as jet fuel prices surgeIn East Africa, the surge has hit carriers hard. Airlines including RwandAir, Ethiopian Airlines, Kenya Airways and its low-cost subsidiary Jambojet have all seen fuel costs surge by up to 70 per cent. Fuel spending is the single largest expense for carriers in the region, and the surge in prices means that fuel now accounts for a larger proportion of airlines’ operational costs this year.

Kenya Airways, for example, reported a 66 per cent increase in fuel spending in the first six months of the year compared to last year, rising from $131 million to $223 million and accounting for 32 per cent of its operating costs, up from 22 per cent last year.

RwandAir said its fuel costs had increased by around 70 per cent and that fuel spending now accounted for around 40 per cent of its costs. Kenya’s Jambojet has reported a similar impact, forcing it to reduce its frequency on some routes.

According to Mr Berthe, African carriers have been hit harder by the fuel crisis because, although their prices are negotiated jointly by the continental association, they import fuel via middlemen. “We work with suppliers who get the fuel from refineries. Currently, we don’t negotiate directly with refineries,” he said.“We need to think about African solutions. The Dangote refinery is providing jet fuel. We need a supplier based in Africa. That would reduce costs.”But it remains unclear to what extent a local refinery could reduce fuel costs for regional airlines. Since Dangote Refinery entered the jet A-1 fuel production market in 2024, West African carriers have not experienced significant cost relief.

Currently, the bulk of Dangote refinery’s jet fuel production, which is about 650,000 barrels per day, is not sufficient to meet West African carriers’ demand. In Nigeria, it has eased supply pressures, but not so much the prices.

Toyin Leo-Olagbaiye, head of aviation at Nigerian energy firm Ardova, said in a recent interview that Dangote Refinery has significantly shielded the Nigerian market from external shocks that previously impacted the aviation fuel market.“Before Dangote came on stream, the Nigerian market was susceptible to two compounding challenges: the price problem and the scarcity problem,” said Mr Leo-Olagbaiye in an interview with Nigerian publication Nairametrics.“Today, while price pressures remain because Dangote still sources part of its crude from the global market, the availability crisis that previously disrupted airline operations has been significantly addressed.”East Africa could have a better success story because Dangote refinery is expected to source most of its crude oil from within the region – from the oil fields in Uganda, South Sudan, and hopefully Kenya and Somalia.

The Nigerian businessman has announced that he expects to break ground in Lamu by the end of this month, bringing the region closer to its first oil refinery, and shining a ray of hope for East Africa’s carriers grappling with costly fuel.

title: ZAWYA: East African airlines carriers count on Dangote Lamu refinery to reduce soaring fuel costs
